# DPDP Act and Employee Background Checks: What Every Indian Company Must Get Right in 2026


September 17, 2026


[Shashank Yadav](https://salarybox.in/blog/author/shashank87cc9f270b/)


[No comments yet](https://salarybox.in/blog/dpdp-act-and-employee-background-checks-what-every-indian-company-must-get-right-in-2026/#respond)


Something changed quietly in Indian hiring over the past year, and a surprising number of companies have not caught up yet.


The Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 is now fully enforceable. That means every time your HR team collects a candidate’s PAN number, Voter ID, Driving Licence, or UAN details during the hiring process, you are handling personal data that falls under specific legal obligations. Consent, storage, access control, and purpose limitation are no longer best practices you can get to someday. They are legal requirements with teeth.


And the teeth are serious. Non compliance penalties under the DPDP Act can reach up to ₹250 crore depending on the severity of the violation. For a startup or mid sized business, even a fraction of that amount would be existential.


So how do you run background checks that actually protect your company without creating the very compliance risk you are trying to avoid? That is what this guide is about.


## What the DPDP Act Actually Requires During Hiring


The DPDP Act introduces several obligations that directly affect how employers conduct background verification. Understanding these is not optional for any company that handles candidate data.


**Explicit consent** must be obtained before you initiate any verification. This means clearly informing the candidate about which checks you plan to run, what data you will access, and how the results will be used. Vague language in an offer letter is not sufficient. The consent needs to be specific and informed.


**Purpose limitation** means you can only use the candidate’s personal data for the purpose it was collected. If you collect a PAN number for identity verification during hiring, you cannot repurpose that data for marketing analytics or share it with unrelated third parties.


**Data minimisation** requires that you only collect the data you actually need. Running unnecessary checks on documents or databases that have no relevance to the role creates unjustified data exposure.


**Security safeguards** must be in place for any personal data you store. Candidate verification records containing PAN numbers, EPFO details, and address information need to be stored securely with appropriate access controls. Leaving verification documents in a shared Google Drive folder that half the company can access is exactly the kind of practice that creates liability.


**Data retention limits** mean you should not hold onto candidate data indefinitely. If a candidate was not hired, their verification data should be retained only as long as your documented retention policy justifies, and then securely disposed of.


## Where Most Companies Go Wrong


The problem is not that companies are deliberately ignoring data protection. The problem is that the way most small and mid sized businesses run background checks was never designed with data protection in mind.


Think about how verification typically works at a growing company. HR collects identity documents over email or WhatsApp. Someone copies the PAN number into a government portal manually. Results are screenshot and dropped into a folder. Employment references are conducted over informal phone calls with no documented consent. Verification records are scattered across email threads, spreadsheets, and chat messages.


Every single step of that process creates a potential DPDP Act violation. Unencrypted transmission. No documented consent. No access control. No retention policy. No audit trail.


The solution is not to stop verifying candidates. It is to verify them through a platform that handles data responsibly by design rather than as an afterthought.

## How to Build a DPDP Compliant Verification Process


You do not need a legal team or a compliance consultant to get this right. Here is a practical framework that works for companies of any size.


Before running any check, include a clear background verification consent clause in your offer letter or application form. State which document checks you will perform and explain that data will be accessed from government databases for identity and employment verification purposes.


Use a structured platform for every verification. Running some checks through a platform and others through manual processes creates inconsistency that is hard to defend during an audit. When every check goes through[Compose1](https://compose1.com/) , you get a consistent workflow, uniform reports, and a single secure location for all records.


Limit access to verification data. Not everyone in your organisation needs to see candidate PAN numbers and employment histories. Restrict access to the people directly involved in hiring decisions.


Define a data retention period. For candidates who were hired, verification records should be retained for the duration of employment and a reasonable period after. For candidates who were not hired, define a shorter retention window and ensure records are disposed of when that window closes.


Document your process. A simple one page policy that outlines your verification steps, consent procedures, access controls, and retention timelines transforms your compliance posture from reactive to proactive.


## The Competitive Advantage of Getting This Right


Here is something that often gets overlooked. DPDP compliance is not just about avoiding penalties. It is a trust signal.


Enterprise clients increasingly ask their vendors and partners about data handling practices during procurement. Investors raise questions about regulatory risk during due diligence. Top candidates are becoming more aware of how their personal data is used during hiring.


A company that can point to a structured, platform based verification process with clean records, documented consent, and secure data handling stands out from competitors who are still running background checks through WhatsApp screenshots and email threads.


## The Bottom Line


The DPDP Act has raised the bar for how Indian companies handle candidate data during hiring. The old way of collecting documents informally, verifying manually, and storing results haphazardly is not just inefficient anymore. It is a legal liability.
